source.title: On the Overlooked Pitfalls of Weight Decay and How to Mitigate Them: A Gradient-Norm Perspective
source.authors: Zeke Xie; Zhi-Qiang Xu; J. Zhang; Issei Sato; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: Supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; no material cut-off noted.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments and theory about how weight decay, optimizer, and its scheduling affect gradient norms, convergence, and test performance. Its results refine the claim that weight decay uniformly improves generalization, but do not test memorization of arbitrary labels or most listed versions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own weight-decay comparisons and measurements of gradient norms, test error, training loss, and Hessian sharpness. Cited results from earlier work are not included. Hyperparameter-selection plots and optimizer comparisons are not separate rows unless they report a direct outcome of weight decay or its schedule.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with momentum SGD on held-out image-classification performance, testing V4 with different weight-decay recipes. Its main gradient-norm and scheduler findings do not by themselves test the other versions. It is not an original source for V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors argue that weight decay can create unstable stationary points and large gradient norms, and that their gradient-norm-aware scheduler mitigates these problems, improves convergence, and often improves held-out performance over constant decay. They conclude that it nearly closes the Adam–SGD performance gap for CNNs. This is qualified by marginal gains over AdamW on ImageNet and failure to outperform conventional L2 regularization on Penn TreeBank.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates weight-decay forms and a new gradient-norm-aware scheduler, comparing Adam, AdamW, AdamS, SGD, and adaptive variants. It does not reproduce the original methods behind the catalog versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by optimizer, dataset/task, weight-decay form and strength, learning-rate schedule, and use of BatchNorm. The authors report AdamS improvements are limited when L2 regularization performs better, especially on Penn TreeBank language modeling.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay increases gradient norms across tested optimizers and architectures, including VGG16 with and without BatchNorm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can increase training-time and final gradient norms under the tested training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: AdamS often improves training loss and held-out image performance over Adam and AdamW, including under cosine schedules; ImageNet improvements over AdamW are marginal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-norm-aware scheduled decay often improves Adam's image-classification performance relative to constant decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Stronger decay increases raw Hessian sharpness, and AdamS reaches flatter solutions than AdamW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-decay form and scheduling affect raw Hessian spectra in the tested ResNet18 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard Adam with L2 regularization outperforms AdamW and AdamS on word-level Penn TreeBank.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The held-out advantage of scheduled or decoupled decay over conventional L2 regularization depends on the task.

fits_no_version.finding: The best of three tested SGD decay strengths scales approximately inversely with epoch count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal SGD weight-decay strength on ResNet18/CIFAR-10 depends on the training duration.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; text also labels the paper arXiv:2011.11152v6, 2024)
record.problems: Claim-relevant generalization evidence is largely optimizer/test-error comparison rather than direct training-versus-test gap measurement. Many learning-curve outcomes are presented only in figures without extractable precise values. Several table comparisons report means and standard deviations from three repeats, but many other results report no uncertainty. The text gives limited detail for several figure settings; batch size is not stated for the gradient-norm plots.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited prior findings and theoretical statements are not experimental outcome rows. Figure 6 comparisons among other adaptive methods are not separately recorded because they do not isolate the claim's specified optimizer comparison as directly as the table and figures above.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels and comparing natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test performance beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures, locality, and convolution-derived initialization.

SGD comparisons on ImageNet and language modeling; equal-or-better training performance of adaptive methods versus SGD; systematic limited-versus-broad tuning comparisons; switching from Adam to SGD. CIFAR tables use default adaptive learning rates and selected SGD learning rates, rather than equally tuning learning rates for every optimizer.
Large-versus-small batches under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for a batch-size penalty.
Dropout ablations, small-data dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and comparison with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Identifying and removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: Add optimizer-specific comparisons with SGD for the unrecorded Table 1 models. VGG16/CIFAR-10: AdamS 6.09, Adam 7.31, AdamW 6.59, SGD 6.42. DenseNet121/CIFAR-100: 20.52, 25.11, 21.55, 19.81. GoogLeNet/CIFAR-100: 21.05, 26.12, 21.29, 21.21. Values are mean test-error percentages, with standard deviations supplied in the table.

Add the unrecorded Table 2 optimizer comparisons. VGG16/CIFAR-10: AdamS 6.16, Adam 7.04, AdamW 6.45, SGD 6.92. ResNet34/CIFAR-100: 23.50, 25.56, 23.61, 24.92. DenseNet121/CIFAR-100: 21.35, 24.39, 22.23, 20.98. GoogLeNet/CIFAR-100: 21.60, 24.60, 21.71, 21.89. These test-error percentages establish model-dependent reversals and residual gaps at the lower decay setting.

record.verdict_notes: All judgments use the supplied text. Mixed optimizer comparisons need separate rows so states can be assigned to individual effects. Rows marked none may describe valid study findings, but their measures do not independently establish a listed version. In particular, Adam-only language-model comparisons do not test Adam versus SGD, and raw Hessian sharpness does not test V7's magnitude-aware measure.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
The paper compares Adam variants and SGD, but does not test the broader claim about limited versus broad optimizer tuning or report language-model results for SGD.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and the comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
